4.2.1 Shrinkage covariance
(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{I} is the Schäfer–Strimmer target D: variances kept, every correlation multiplied by 1-\lambda (Schäfer and Strimmer 2005) TODO-cite: Schäfer and Strimmer 2005, target D; p. to check. \lambda, the shrinkage intensity, is chosen on held-out cells (Section 4.3), either per type or as one level common to the types of a time. The closed-form level is archived (Section 4.2.4). The estimate is positive definite for every \lambda>0, whatever C_j and G_t; the smallest level of the grid is 10^{-3}. The theory is in 3.2, shrinkage.


4.2.2 Two-parameter shrinkage
\bar{\boldsymbol{R}} is the correlation of \boldsymbol{W}=\sum_j (C_j-1)\boldsymbol{V}_j/(N-J), with \boldsymbol{V}_j the sample covariance of type j and N the cells of the J types of one time and one gene set (pooled_correlation()). \boldsymbol{W} is the tied covariance of linear discriminant analysis. \alpha moves \boldsymbol{R}_j towards \bar{\boldsymbol{R}}; \lambda then moves the result towards \boldsymbol{I}. This is the family of regularised discriminant analysis TODO-cite: Friedman 1989, Regularized discriminant analysis, Journal of the American Statistical Association; p. to check TODO-cite: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer; ch. 4, sec. 4.3.1, p. 112, eqs. 4.13–4.14. In cross-validation \bar{\boldsymbol{R}} never contains the held-out cells of the type being scored.
\bar{\boldsymbol{R}} alone is not an arm. It has G_t(G_t-1)/2 free correlations, 0.9 to 17.4 million, for 4,611 to 10,891 cells per time. At 96 h it is singular: \boldsymbol{W} has rank at most N-J = 4,930, for 5,893 genes. It enters only as a target, with \alpha<1 and \lambda>0.


4.2.3 Factor analysis
fit_factor_correlation() fits \boldsymbol{R}_j\approx\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j with q_j factors by maximum likelihood, with the EM steps of Rubin and Thayer TODO-cite: Rubin and Thayer 1982, EM algorithms for ML factor analysis, Psychometrika; p. to check. The columns of \boldsymbol{B}_j are the factor loadings and the diagonal \boldsymbol{\Psi}_j holds the uniquenesses. The steps are written on the cells, so the G\times G correlation is never formed. The cells are standardised with the Poisson floor of Section 4.3. The start is the probabilistic PCA solution; EM stops after 200 steps. Uniquenesses are floored at 0.01: with fewer cells than genes the likelihood is unbounded when one of them tends to zero. Rank 0 is the diagonal model.
fit_factor_shared() fits \boldsymbol{R}_j\approx\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j: the types of one time share the loadings and keep their own uniquenesses (“same axes, own volumes”). It alternates closed-form updates of the rows of \boldsymbol{B} and of each \boldsymbol{\Psi}_j, for at most 100 steps.
A factor model on G genes has G+qG-q(q-1)/2 free covariance parameters: loadings up to rotation, plus uniquenesses TODO-cite: Murphy 2012, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press; ch. 12, sec. 12.1.3, p. 384. Shared loadings are counted once, plus one uniqueness vector per type. A rank is used only if it is at most the training cells minus two, at most the rank of the training correlation, and leaves no more parameters than the G(G+1)/2 entries of the matrix. Rank 30 is therefore never fitted for the 29-cell somite differentiation front.


4.2.4 Archived arms
These arms are not run in the current pipeline. Their code and a README are in scripts/archives/sparse_precision_arms/ and scripts/archives/denoised_covariance/.
Sparse precisions. The graphical lasso with an unpenalised diagonal (glasso, EBIC path), the SILGGM support with a refit, and PLNnetwork, a Poisson log-normal model with the full-library offset \log s_c and a latent precision \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_z^{-1} penalised off the diagonal:

x_{gc}\mid\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(s_{c}e^{z_{gc}}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{z}_{\cdot c}\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{z},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{z}).
\tag{4.4}
None was run on the gated panel. The pipeline now regularises covariances only; these precision estimators may return as a sensitivity analysis. Theory: 3.2, graphical lasso, 3.2, PLN.

Denoised covariance. The Poisson diagonal and a share \kappa of the size term removed from the sample covariance, \kappa bracketed between 0 and \hat\nu/(1+\hat\nu), with \hat\nu from extrinsic_noise_nu() (3.2, raw or denoised). It gave the worst deconvolution of the second pass: RMSE 0.47 at 96 h, Welch panel. These second-pass results are kept in output/deconvolution/second_pass/ and are still read by



Closed-form shrinkage level. The Schäfer–Strimmer \hat\lambda^{\ast} of corpcor minimises a Frobenius risk, not the Gaussian likelihood that DeCovarT evaluates. In the first pass it was 0.006 to 0.026 for the 3 units with 3,589 cells or more, and 0.60 to 0.74 for the units with 29 to 66 cells (output/deconvolution/second_pass/plugin_summary_first_pass.csv).

title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.3 Cross-validation and outputs
One loss selects every tuning value and compares the arms: the held-out Gaussian log-score on the linear scale. For held-out cells \mathcal{T} and an estimate (\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}) fitted without them,

\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}};\mathcal{T})
=
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{T}}
\log\phi_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot c};\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\bigr).
\tag{4.5}
Its expectation is maximised at the true mean and covariance whatever the law of the cells (Stein’s loss), so it is a legitimate loss even though cells are not Gaussian (3.2, Gaussian log-score). Why it replaces AIC, BIC and EBIC as the selector is in 3.2, cross-validation. The bulk samples are never read.
Folds. Leave-one-out under 100 cells (the 36 and 66 naïve cells at 48 h and 72 h, the 29-cell somite front), 5-fold otherwise. The two-parameter arm uses 5 folds in every unit. Shared loadings use 5 joint folds, each type split into 5. Folds split the cells of one unit: the score measures generalisation to new cells of this specimen, not to new specimens (Note 3.1).
TODO (reply to Elias, 2026-11-22): complement the held-out log-score by the universal approximate cross-validation (UACV) of Commenges et al. (2015), which approximates leave-one-out without refitting and corrects for a misspecified or penalised fit, and report its tracking interval \Delta_{\mathrm{UACV}}\pm1.96\,\hat\omega/\sqrt{n} when two arms or two models are compared. The interval is asymptotic only, and its unit must be an independent one: cells of one specimen are pseudo-replicates, and three bulk replicates per time are too few for a stable variance.
Poisson floor. split_standardise() (R/03_01_stats_covariance_estimation.R) standardises the training and test cells with the training mean \bar x_g and standard deviation s_g of each gene, with the variance floored at its Poisson level plus one count over the C_{\mathrm{tr}} training cells:

s_g^{2}=\max\Bigl(v_g,\ \bar x_g+\tfrac{1}{C_{\mathrm{tr}}}\Bigr),
\tag{4.6}
with v_g the sample variance. A count cannot vary less than a Poisson count; a smaller variance means too few cells, or the fractional counts left by ambient-RNA correction. The floor replaced a defect found in the shared-loadings arm. Before it, the held-out score of the 29-cell somite differentiation front at 96 h (outer fold 2 of the nested comparison) was about -5\times10^{10}. The gene Fnbp1 has fractional ambient-corrected counts in that type: training mean 4\times10^{-7}, standard deviation 1.9\times10^{-6}. One count in a test cell then cost about 6\times10^{11}. With the floor that fold scores −9,260, and the other types move by less than 0.3%. These values come from the diagnosis of the defect, not from the tables below. The factor fits use the same scale (build_sigma(), Section 4.2); the shrinkage plug-in of the deconvolution is unchanged. The tables of Section 4.4 come from the rerun with the floor (24 November 2026, 15:49).
One spectral decomposition per training set. The test cells are standardised with the training means and the floored standard deviations s_g of Equation 4.6. Let \boldsymbol{R}=\sum_{i\le r}\ell_i\boldsymbol{v}_i\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top} be the training correlation, of rank r on G genes. The eigenvectors of (1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}+\lambda\boldsymbol{I} do not depend on \lambda; its eigenvalues are e_i=(1-\lambda)\ell_i+\lambda on the range and \lambda on the null space. For a standardised test cell \boldsymbol{z},

\log\phi
=
-\tfrac12\Bigl[
G\log 2\pi+2\sum_g\log s_g
+\sum_{i\le r}\log e_i+(G-r)\log\lambda
+\sum_{i\le r}\frac{(\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{z})^{2}}{e_i}
+\frac{\lVert\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}-\sum_{i\le r}(\boldsymbol{v}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{z})^{2}}{\lambda}
\Bigr].
\tag{4.7}

One decomposition therefore scores the 43 levels (spectral_path_core()). It is taken on the smaller of \boldsymbol{Z}\boldsymbol{Z}^{\top} and \boldsymbol{Z}^{\top}\boldsymbol{Z}, with \boldsymbol{Z} the standardised training cells. The two-parameter arm needs one decomposition per \alpha.
Factor scores. With \boldsymbol{M}=\boldsymbol{I}+\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}, of size q\times q,

(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi})^{-1}
=
\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{M}^{-1}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Psi}^{-1},
\qquad
\det(\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi})
=
\det\boldsymbol{\Psi}\,\det\boldsymbol{M}
\tag{4.8}

(factor_core()). No G\times G matrix is factorised.
Constant genes. A gene constant in a training set is scored apart, as an independent Gaussian with the variance of Equation 4.6. That part of the score is the same for every tuning value; it is left out of the fold-to-fold spread.
Rules.

Per type: the value with the highest mean held-out score (min). The one-standard-error choice, the most regularised value within one standard error of that maximum, is reported beside it (1se).
Common: one value per time, the one with the highest sum over types of the mean held-out score. For shared loadings this is the only rule.

Nested comparison. A nested cross-validation: the cells of each time are split into 5 outer folds, stratified by type. Each rule chooses its tuning value on the outer training cells only, with the folds above, and is scored on the outer test cells. Scores are paired by fold and type; the gain is reported against the diagonal model.
Information criteria. The factor models are refitted on all cells of each unit (stage fit; these fits enter the deconvolution). AIC and BIC are computed from the free-parameter counts of Table 4.3, plus G means per type. They are reported, not used to select.
Grid search only. Every tuning value is chosen on a fixed grid. With one or two tuning parameters a grid is as reliable as random search, whose advantage appears when few of many hyperparameters matter TODO-cite: Bergstra and Bengio 2012, Random search for hyper-parameter optimization, Journal of Machine Learning Research 13:281–305; p. 283. Here the shrinkage “path” is itself a grid, of 43 levels, scored from one spectral decomposition per fold (Equation 4.7); the two-parameter arm adds one decomposition per \alpha. The former search stage compared, on 5 folds, the exact path on 200 levels, a 10-value grid with one Cholesky factor per value, optimize() on the path over [10^{-3},1] and 10 random levels; for the two-parameter arm, on panels of at most 1,500 genes, a 5\times8 grid in (\alpha,\lambda) against 40 random pairs. It is archived in scripts/archives/search_comparison/ (see its README); its table, output/grn/cv/search_comparison.csv, is still read here (Section 4.4.3). The loss of a strategy is the held-out score of the best path value minus that of its choice.


\begin{algorithm} \caption{Held-out scores along the paths, selection, and nested comparison} \begin{algorithmic} \Procedure{PathScores}{$X_{\mathrm{train}}, X_{\mathrm{test}}, \Lambda, Q, A$} \State standardise both sets with the training means and standard deviations \State $(\ell, V) \gets$ non-zero spectrum of the training correlation $R$ \For{$\lambda \in \Lambda$} \State $s(\lambda) \gets$ mean path score of the test cells, from $(\ell, V)$ \EndFor \For{$q \in Q$} \State $(B, \Psi) \gets$ \Call{FactorEM}{$X_{\mathrm{train}}, q$}, started from $(\ell, V)$ \State $s(q) \gets$ mean test score through the Woodbury identity \EndFor \For{$\alpha \in A$} \State spectrum of $(1-\alpha)R + \alpha\bar R$; $s(\alpha,\lambda)$ for every $\lambda \in \Lambda$ \EndFor \State \Return $s$ \EndProcedure \Procedure{Select}{$X$, folds} \For{each fold $k$} \State $s_k \gets$ \Call{PathScores}{$X_{-k}, X_k, \Lambda, Q, A$} \EndFor \State $m \gets$ mean of $s_k$ over folds \State \Return $\arg\max m$ per type; $\arg\max \sum_j m_j$ for a common value \EndProcedure \Procedure{NestedCompare}{$X_1,\ldots,X_J$} \State split each $X_j$ into 5 outer folds \For{$k = 1,\ldots,5$} \For{each rule $e$} \State choose its value by \Call{Select}{} on the outer training cells \State $g_{ek} \gets$ test score of rule $e$ $-$ test score of the diagonal \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $(g_{ek})$, paired by fold \EndProcedure \end{algorithmic} \end{algorithm}


Outputs in output/grn/cv/:

cv_tuning_scores.csv: mean and standard error of the held-out score for each unit, arm and tuning value;
cv_selected_tuning.csv: the value chosen by each rule (Table 4.4);
nested_cv_by_fold.csv, nested_cv_summary.csv: outer-fold scores and gains over the diagonal (Table 4.6);
information_criteria.csv: log-likelihood, parameters, AIC, BIC and EM convergence per factor rank;
search_comparison.csv: choice, loss and time of each search strategy (Table 4.7), written by the archived search stage and not rewritten by the current script.

Every file covers the three panels. Table 4.4 and Table 4.6 show the Welch panel; Table 4.5 gives the choices made once per time on all three.

For the arm and tuning value retained, \widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} is the mean of the raw counts of the cells of type j, and \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} is Equation 4.3, both on the scale of Section 4.1.1. It is positive definite because \lambda>0 or \boldsymbol{\Psi}_j\succ0, so Equation 4.1 holds by construction. Which covariance layer these cell-level moments identify, and how the sample scales are estimated inside the DeCovarT fit, is in 2.1, three regimes and 2.1, profile Newton.

4.4 Results and discussion

4.4.1 Regularisation shrinks covariance terms without setting them to zero
What the shrinkage arm returns. The estimate is \boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}\{(1-\lambda)\boldsymbol{R}_j+\lambda\boldsymbol{I}\}\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2} (Section 4.2.1). Three readings follow.

Variances are untouched. Only the correlations move.
Every correlation is multiplied by 1-\lambda; none becomes zero. The estimate has as many non-zero off-diagonal terms as the sample covariance: all G_t(G_t-1)/2 pairs, that is 0.9 million at 48 h, 6.5 million at 72 h and 17.4 million at 96 h on the Welch panel. Its inverse is dense as well, so no graph can be read from either matrix. The factor models are dense too: each off-diagonal term is an entry of \boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}.
\lambda is a floor on the spectrum. Each eigenvalue \ell of \boldsymbol{R}_j becomes (1-\lambda)\ell+\lambda, so the smallest eigenvalue of the shrunk correlation is at least \lambda. That floor makes the estimate positive definite when C_j\le G_t.

A dense estimate is not evidence that every pair of genes interacts. Three mechanisms give a non-zero covariance to a pair with no direct link.

Sampling noise. A sample correlation is never exactly zero, even for independent genes. Shrinkage multiplies it by 1-\lambda; it does not threshold.
Covariance is not the network. Direct interactions are the zeros of the precision matrix. Two genes linked only through other genes still have a non-zero covariance. title: 4  Covariance estimation
text:
4.5 Glossary
The terms underlined in this chapter, with the definitions of glossary/glossary.yml.




Table 4.8: Glossary of the terms used in this chapter.






term
definition




arm
One way of regularising the covariance of each cell type, with its own tuning value: shrinkage towards the variances, the two-parameter family, or a factor model. The deconvolution model stays the same in every arm.


capture ratio
The factor that takes a reference count onto the scale of the bulk. The mean grows with the product of this factor and the cell count. The within-type covariance grows with its square times the cell count.


cell count
The number n of cells whose transcripts make up one bulk sample. It is not measured for the Suppinger bulks, so it is only known through c and phi.


cell size
The total transcript content of a cell. Its counts are the biological size times the technical capture, so the two cannot be told apart from counts alone.


deviance share
The fraction of a gene's Poisson deviance explained by the cell types, written R2_D. The panels keep the Welch-gated genes with R2_D of at least 1% or 5%.


factor loading
A column of the matrix B in the covariance B B' + Psi: the weights with which one latent factor moves the genes together.


Frobenius risk
The expected sum, over every gene pair, of the squared error of that covariance entry. A variance and a covariance count the same.


grid search
Scoring every value of a fixed list of tuning values and keeping the best. With one or two tuning parameters it is as reliable as random search.


held-out log-score
The Gaussian log-density of cells left out of the fit, averaged over them. A higher value means the covariance estimated without them predicts them better.


mean scale
The number c that takes the reference mixture mean to the scale of the bulk. Physically, the capture ratio times the number of cells in the bulk, c = a n.


nested cross-validation
Two loops of cross-validation: the inner loop chooses the tuning value on the training cells only, and the outer loop scores that choice on cells the inner loop never saw.


Poisson floor
The smallest variance accepted for a gene in a held-out score: its mean plus one count over the number of training cells, since a count cannot vary less than a Poisson count.


RMSE
Root mean squared error between estimated and observed proportions, over the cell types of a sample.


shrinkage intensity
The number between 0 and 1 that multiplies the sample correlations of a type. At 0 they are kept. At 1 only the variances remain.


size factor
The multiplier of a cell's whole library: the number of transcripts the cell holds (biological) times the fraction of them that the protocol captures and sequences (technical). It moves every gene of the cell together.


uniqueness
The diagonal Psi of a factor model: the variance of each gene that the shared factors do not explain.


variance scale
The number phi that multiplies the mixture covariance of the reference to give the covariance of the bulk. Physically, phi = a squared times n.


Welch panel
The genes that differ between cell types by a permuted Welch test at a false discovery rate of 5%, after the presence gate. The largest of the three gene panels.

Schäfer, Juliane, and Korbinian Strimmer. 2005. “A Shrinkage Approach to Large-Scale Covariance Matrix Estimation and Implications for Functional Genomics.” Statistical Applications in Genetics and Molecular Biology 4: Article32. https://doi.org/10.2202/1544-6115.1175.

title: 5  Applying and comparing deconvolution outputs applied to Suppinger study
text:
The chapter asks whether a per-type covariance improves deconvolution of the Suppinger bulk samples (GSE229386, 48, 72 and 96 h, three standard-Wnt replicates per time) against mean-based methods, when every method receives the same genes and the same scored cells.
One DeCovarT model is fitted throughout (single-cell law, raw-count covariances, profiled scales, L-BFGS-B); only the regularisation of the within-type correlation moves, and its level is chosen by the bulk likelihood summed over the replicates, never by the observed composition. The observed composition is the share of scored cells in the single-cell annotation.
On the Welch panel, with shrinkage of the raw covariance, the bulk likelihood chooses 0.1 at 48 h, 0.5 at 72 h and 0.5 at 96 h; the RMSE there is 0.021 at 48 h, 0.043 at 72 h and 0.034 at 96 h. The best comparator at 96 h is MEAD (pseudo-individuals) (0.048).
At 96 h most of the remaining error is a split inside paraxial mesoderm, whose mean profiles are nearly collinear (Table 5.9); the bulk is far from the reference mixture on many genes (Table 5.10).
The bulk likelihood ranks levels within one covariance family; across families a higher likelihood is not a lower error (Section 5.3.8). Factor analysis needs positive scales (Section 5.3.4).
Limits: three replicates per protocol and time, no interval on a chosen level, one reference per time. The smaller gene panels and the case where each method selects its own genes are in the appendix (Section 5.6, Section 5.5).

5.2 What is being compared
Numbers to rerun: they were computed on the panel of the earlier tier (i), which dropped the 2,178 mostly fractional genes and used the 5 % presence gate. Tier (i) now keeps every gene and applies the gate of Equation 3.1 (Section 3.2.1).
DeCovarT deconvolves bulk profiles with both a mean signature and a per-type covariance. Every method below uses the same gene panel and the same labelled single-cell reference; they differ in what they model beyond the mean. They estimate the proportion of each scored type, a share of cells. All runs are planned on GSE229386, at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, for the standard Wnt pulse and the early pulse (Section 2.1). Each model is reviewed in 5.1, review; one line here says what it models and how it is called.

5.2.1 Second-generation, mean-based

BayesPrism (Chu et al. 2022) — a multinomial likelihood on bulk counts with the single-cell reference as a prior on cell-type expression, updated by Gibbs sampling. R, BayesPrism: new.prism(), run.prism(), get.fraction().
SCDC (Dong et al. 2021) — weighted non-negative least squares with clipped gene weights, and an ensemble over several references. With one reference the ensemble step does nothing. R, SCDC: SCDC_prop(), or SCDC_prop_ONE() for a one-subject reference.
DWLS (Tsoucas et al. 2019) TODO-cite: Tsoucas et al. 2019, dampened weighted least squares; p. to check — dampened weighted least squares, weights the inverse squared fitted mean, capped by a dampening constant. R, DWLS: solveDampenedWLS().
DeMixSC TODO-cite: Guo et al. 2025, DeMixSC, Genome Research 35:147–161; pp. 150, 157 — weighted non-negative least squares whose gene weights are rebuilt from the residuals, with a down-weighted set G_2 of genes that differ between a bulk and a single-nucleus library of one aliquot. Run here twice: the weights alone (deconvolute_demixsc_wnnls(), G_2 empty) and the package aligned on pseudo-bulks of the other two times (deconvolute_demixsc_aligned(), Section 5.2.6).
DECALS (Cai et al. 2024, 6–7 of the author manuscript) — constrained least squares on relative abundances, with a sandwich variance that carries a covariance per type. The authors release no code; it is re-implemented in deconvolute_decals() (R/04_01_stats_deconvolution.R).

TODO-cite: Chu et al. 2022 (BayesPrism, key chuCellTypeGeneExpression2022), p. to check, and Dong et al. 2021 (SCDC, key dongSCDCBulkGene2021), p. to check; both in DeCovarT inst/REFERENCES.bib, not in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib.


5.2.2 Single-cell likelihood strategy

DeCovarT, profile Newton — the linear single-cell layer, with \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{W,j} weighted by p_{ji} and both sample scales profiled out, maximised by trust-region Newton in ILR coordinates (2.1, profile Newton). R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell(optimiser = "newton").
DeCovarT, Levenberg–Marquardt — the released population convolution, covariance \sum_j p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j, maximised by marqLevAlg in ILR coordinates. With a one-specimen reference the quadratic slot is the wrong one (2.1, one replicate); the fit is the reference point for the released model. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_Marquardt_Levenberg().
RNA-Sieve (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 1802–5) — genes independent; a central-limit Gaussian bulk whose variance is linear in the cell count, with the reference means as noisy regressors and Godambe (sandwich) intervals. Python, rnasieve (songlab-cal/rna-sieve): model_from_raw_counts(), then predict(), called by scripts/python/run_rnasieve.py, which repairs the simplex-constrained update of the released package (Section 5.2.6).
MEAD (Xie and Wang 2023, 8–9 and 13 of arXiv:2202.06420v5) — an estimating equation corrected for reference measurement error, with gene–gene dependence in the sandwich variance and intervals for \boldsymbol{p}. R, MEAD (DongyueXie/MEAD): MEAD().
ReDeconv (Lu et al. 2025, 4 and 14) — keeps the transcriptome size S_j in the reference, corrects gene length on the bulk side only, and models the within-type variance through a central-limit law over cells. Code jyyulab/redeconv, called by scripts/python/run_redeconv.py (ReDeconv()).



5.2.3 Gold-standard baselines

NNLS — non-negative least squares on the mean signature, then projection on the simplex; homoscedastic, mean only. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_nnls(), which calls nnls::nnls().
Robust linear regression (RLM) — Huber M-estimation of \boldsymbol{y}\approx\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, which down-weights outlying genes. R: DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_rlm(), which calls MASS::rlm(method = "M").

DeMixSC needs a bulk and a single-nucleus library of one aliquot TODO-cite: Guo et al. 2025, DeMixSC, Genome Research 35:147–161; pp. 149, 156. The aligned run takes, for time t, the standard-Wnt bulks of the two other times, each paired with a pseudo-bulk of its own time (leave one time out; nothing of time t enters the alignment). Its ComBat step assumes that benchmark and target bulks share a tissue environment TODO-cite: Guo et al. 2025, DeMixSC, Genome Research 35:147–161; p. 151; bulks of other developmental times do not, so the alignment also removes the expression changes between times that carry the composition.
DECALS needs many bulks to estimate its type covariances (Cai et al. 2024, 3, 8–9 of the author manuscript). The paper regresses residual cross-products on squared proportions across bulks, with a finite-sample bias correction (eqs. 6–9, pp. 8–9; proof pp. S27–S28), then thresholds the correlations by SCAD with a cross-validated threshold and takes the nearest positive semi-definite matrix (pp. S1–S2). With three bulks per time, deconvolute_decals() takes the reference covariance of each type, carried to the relative scale by the delta method, with one variance scale per sample; the bias correction, which acts on that regression only, has no counterpart.

Design.

One gene panel for every method: RNA-Sieve’s off-simplex and outlier filters (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 1803–4), MEAD’s gene filter, ReDeconv’s selection of about 100 signature genes per type by t-test, fold change and lowest coefficient of variation (Lu et al. 2025, 14) are off. RNA-Sieve runs without library normalisation, so its estimand stays a cell fraction.
DeMixSC runs on the panel: about 63% of the panel genes (62–64% by time, in the check run) fall in the down-weighted set G_2, which a weight of 10^{-6} almost discards.
DECALS works on panel shares of UMI counts, not on FPKM divided by the total over all genes (p. S1); its estimate is converted to cell fractions with the panel total per cell of each type, which the paper does not do. Intervals are clipped to [0,1], which the paper does not do either; at a face of the simplex the point estimate stays the constrained fit of eq. 3, as in Algorithm 1 (p. 9), and the variance is that of Theorem 1 (p. S22).

Package against paper.

MEAD_getX divides every cell by its total, which the paper avoids (Xie and Wang 2023, PDF p. 35, Remark S2); the estimate is converted from transcript to cell shares. Not fixed: it would mean rewriting an unexported function.
DeMixSC computes its later weights in the weighted space, adds a fold-change cut-off and scales each bulk to 10^5, none of which the paper states; the unaligned run follows eq. 4 on raw counts.
ReDeconv runs six reweighted, unconstrained least squares, then clips and rescales, where the paper maximises a likelihood (Lu et al. 2025, 14).

Fixed here.

RNA-Sieve’s simplex-constrained update. In rnasieve 0.1.4 the update passes its constraints to cp.Minimize() instead of cp.Problem(). Under the pinned cvxpy 1.6.0 that raises a TypeError, which the package catches; the proportions then never move, and predict() returns a clipped and rescaled weighted least squares, not the maximiser of Algorithm 1 (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 1804). scripts/python/run_rnasieve.py installs the corrected update (--release restores the released behaviour).
RNA-Sieve intervals. The runner now reports the Godambe intervals of the paper (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 1805). With near-collinear types the package returns [0,1] when its averaged Hessian is ill-conditioned.
DECALS re-implemented. No public code exists; the point estimate is the constrained least squares of the paper and the interval the sandwich of Theorem 1 (p. S22), mapped to cell fractions by the delta method. Checked against the supplement: \boldsymbol{U}, \boldsymbol{D} and the projection of Lemma S1 (p. S23) match. The fallback without reference covariances used p-K+1 degrees of freedom for \sigma_i^2; it now uses p-1, the starting value of Algorithm 1 (p. 9). The runs with reference covariances are unchanged.

5.3 Statistical interpretation of the results
Two scenarios answer different questions. When each method chooses its own genes, a difference between two methods mixes the gene set, the input scale and the estimator; that scenario, and the hypothesis it suggests, is in the appendix (Section 5.5). This chapter gives every method the same genes, so a difference comes from the estimator alone.
The runs of this book give every method the same genes, the same scored cells and raw counts (scripts/04_01_stats_deconvolution.R):

panels per time: the Welch panel and its subsets with a deviance share R^2_D\ge 5\% and, in the current run, R^2_D\ge 1\% (Section 3.3, Section 4.1.1);
the solver of each method, called directly, without its own marker step: DWLS::solveDampenedWLS() on the mean signature, SCDC::SCDC_prop_ONE(), BayesPrism with its outlier filter off, rnasieve (repaired in the current run), the DeMixSC weighted NNLS and, in the current run, the aligned DeMixSC weights and DECALS (Section 5.2.6);
DeCovarT with four covariance inputs, with and without the gene-wise platform ratio, and two optimisers (second pass), then along the levels of each arm and under four scale models (current run, Section 5.3.3, Section 5.3.5).

A difference between methods is then a difference between estimators. A difference between panels, for one method, measures what the gene set contributes. If the hypothesis of Section 5.5 holds, DWLS on the shared panel should move towards SCDC and BayesPrism.
The second pass (11 November 2026) adds to that list MEAD with four pseudo-individuals per type, ReDeconv on supplied moments, robust linear regression (DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_rlm()), and four diagnostic families written in R/04_02_stats_sieve_multivariate.R: a multivariate RNA-Sieve, DeCovarT at other shrinkage levels, DeCovarT with the between-type covariance term, and Firth-penalised DeCovarT.

No optimiser failure. The gain is never negative: the estimate is a better maximum of the objective than the observed composition, by about 1,100 units at 96 h on the Welch panel. L-BFGS-B works on non-negative weights, not on ILR coordinates.
Which term carries the gain depends on the covariance. With the denoised covariance on the Welch panel at 72 h and 96 h it is the log-determinant; with the raw covariance at 96 h it is the quadratic term, and the log-determinant goes the other way. My first reading, from one sample, generalised the denoised case too far.
Why the log-determinant can matter at all. \log\det is concave on positive definite matrices (ledger L1, numeric). When two covariances have complementary near-null directions of size \varepsilon, mixing them raises \log\det by about -\log\varepsilon (ledger L2). The denoised covariance of a type with C_j cells has rank at most C_j-1 before shrinkage (1,382 of 1,417 eigenvalues clipped to zero for the 36 naïve cells at 48 h, first pass), so a vertex has a much smaller determinant than a mixture.
Why profiling makes both terms comparable. The quadratic form enters Equation 5.1 through its logarithm. Its gradient is the fixed-scale gradient divided by \hat\phi (ledger P3), and \hat\phi is 10^6 to 10^8 here. A model with one scale for mean and variance, as RNA-Sieve, keeps the quadratic form at full weight.

Same plug-ins, quadratic programme instead of likelihood. The multivariate RNA-Sieve (fit_sieve_chain()) writes the bulk as \boldsymbol{y}\sim\mathcal{N}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{w},\,
n\,\boldsymbol{S}_T(\boldsymbol{p})\bigr), one n for the mean and the covariance. Its covariance is that of a bulk whose cell-type counts are multinomial (ledger C1, C2):

\boldsymbol{S}_T(\boldsymbol{p})
=\sum_j p_j\bigl(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j
+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}\bigr)
-(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}
=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})
+\sum_j p_j(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})
(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p})^{\top}.
\tag{5.2}
The second term is the covariance of the type a random cell belongs to. It does not correlate the cell types with one another; it has rank at most J-1. DeCovarT’s \boldsymbol{S}_W omits it, which holds the number of cells of each type fixed. RNA-Sieve states the diagonal of Equation 5.2; the matrix form is derived here.
Six stages are stored for each of three covariance inputs (diagonal of the raw covariance, full raw, full denoised):

qp_within: freeze the covariance, solve \min_{\boldsymbol{w}\ge 0}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{w})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{U}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{w}) with quadprog::solve.QP(), update the covariance, repeat; then \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}=\boldsymbol{w}/\sum_j w_j. Within-type covariance only.
qp: the same with \boldsymbol{S}_T.
qp_huber: qp with Huber weights on the whitened residuals.
qp_means: qp alternated with the closed-form refinement of the means, per bulk (ledger S1), \boldsymbol{m}_j=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}
+(w_j/C_j)\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j(\boldsymbol{U}+\boldsymbol{Q})^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{w}), \boldsymbol{Q}=\sum_j(w_j^{2}/C_j)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j.
qp_means_var: adds d_g, the mean over the six bulks of a time of the squared residual over the model variance (the diagonal of the DECALS moment regression; correlations kept from the reference).
full_lik: from that state, the full likelihood with its log-determinant, maximised in \boldsymbol{w}\ge 0.


The estimating equation is what differs. On the Welch panel at 96 h, with the full raw covariance, the QP gives 0.060 and its iteration converges for the three replicates. DeCovarT with the same covariance gives 0.36 (Figure 5.16, appendix). The QP uses the covariance as a weight only; the likelihood also reads the composition from it.
The between-type term changes little: qp_within and qp have the same RMSE to the third decimal in 10 of the 18 cells of Figure 5.16, and differ by at most 0.05.
Refining the means from one bulk fails. The RMSE rises to 0.50 at 96 h and to 0.76 at 72 h on the Welch panel; the refined profiles move by 20 to 100% of their norm (mean over the six bulks of a chain). One bulk has G values for JG means, so the bulk is fitted by the profiles instead of the proportions. RNA-Sieve shares the refined means across bulks; that version was not written here, and six bulks with two protocols would still be few for three to five profiles.
The gene-wise variance scale has no consistent effect (worse at 96 h on the Welch panel; the small panel is in the appendix), and the alternation did not converge in 13 of 18 chains.
The full likelihood undoes the QP on the Welch panel with the full raw covariance (0.060 → 0.47 at 96 h, starting from refined means).
The denoised covariance alone is unstable: its QP iteration does not converge at 96 h on the Welch panel (nor on the smaller one). It is a fixed point, not a descent, and a nearly singular weight matrix makes it cycle.

The released Python RNA-Sieve behaved as a weighted least squares in the second pass. In rnasieve 0.1.4 the proportion update passes its simplex constraints to cp.Minimize() instead of cp.Problem(); under the pinned cvxpy 1.6.0 that call raises a TypeError, which the package catches and answers with the previous proportions (checked on a toy). Lines 6 and 12 of Algorithm 1 (Erdmann-Pham et al. 2021, 1804) then never move the composition, and predict() returns a clipped and rescaled weighted least squares. The RNA-Sieve rows of this section are that released estimator. scripts/python/run_rnasieve.py now installs the corrected update and reports the Godambe intervals (Section 5.2.6); the current run (Section 5.3.3) uses the repaired estimator.
Shrinkage level of the raw covariance. rescale_shrinkage() moves the raw covariance to another \lambda by multiplying its off-diagonal terms by (1-\lambda)/(1-\hat\lambda^{\ast}_j) (ledger S2); variances are untouched.

Abundant types get \lambda\approx 0.02 and rare ones 0.6: the weight matrices of the types are then of very different quality, and the likelihood reads that difference as signal. One common, larger \lambda removes it. This is an interpretation; the sweep does not separate “larger” from “common”.

5.3.4 Positivity of the mean scale
The factor arm stops when the generalised least-squares mean scale is not positive (Section 5.3.3), although every covariance it uses is positive definite. Three requirements are at stake, and they are distinct. Local symbols of this section and the next: \boldsymbol{m}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p}, the mixture mean; \boldsymbol{W}, a precision; N, D, Q, the whitened products of Equation 5.4 and Equation 5.7; \nu and \boldsymbol{\Delta}, the variance of the size factor and the rest of the covariance; c_{\min}, the floor of the positive scale; A_{jk}, the alignment of loading k of type j with its mean.

A positive definite covariance, \boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{x}>0 for every \boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{0}. It allows negative covariances between genes.
Non-negative means, \mu_{gj}\ge 0: an order constraint in the positive orthant, with no direct link to the first.
A positive scale, c=a\,n>0 (the capture ratio times the cell count). A scalar parameter needs its own constraint or parameterisation.

The factor covariance is positive definite by construction. With \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j=\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}(\boldsymbol{B}_j\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi}_j)\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}, \boldsymbol{D}_j diagonal positive and every uniqueness \psi_{jg}>0, put \boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{D}_j^{1/2}\boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{0}:

\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j\boldsymbol{x}
=\lVert\boldsymbol{B}_j^{\top}\boldsymbol{z}\rVert^{2}
+\sum_g\psi_{jg}z_g^{2}>0 ,
\tag{5.3}
the low-rank-plus-diagonal form of factor analysis TODO-cite: Murphy 2012, Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective, MIT Press; ch. 12, sec. 12.1.1, p. 382, eq. 12.6. The uniquenesses are floored at 0.01 in the fits (Section 4.2.3). A mixture \boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})=\sum_jp_j\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_j with p_j\ge0, \sum_jp_j=1 is then positive definite on the whole simplex. A low-rank matrix alone, \boldsymbol{U}_r\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_r\boldsymbol{U}_r^{\top} with r<G, has G-r zero eigenvalues; a likelihood that needs \boldsymbol{S}^{-1} and \log\det\boldsymbol{S} needs the diagonal term. How other latent factor models (MOFA, non-negative factorisations) separate signed factors from a positive observation model is discussed in the DeCovarT vignette 3.2.
A positive definite covariance does not give a positive scale. At a composition \boldsymbol{p}, with \boldsymbol{m}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p} and \boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p})^{-1}, the free scale is

\hat c=\frac{N}{D},\qquad
N=\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{y},\qquad
D=\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m}.
\tag{5.4}
D>0 always; N need not be. With \boldsymbol{W}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\-2&5\end{pmatrix} (leading minors 1 and 1, so positive definite), \boldsymbol{m}=(1,1)^{\top} and \boldsymbol{y}=(10,1)^{\top}, both positive, \boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{y}=(8,-15)^{\top} and N=-7. A positive definite \boldsymbol{W} makes \langle\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{u}\rangle_W>0, not \langle\boldsymbol{u},\boldsymbol{v}\rangle_W>0 for two different positive vectors: \hat c<0 means that the bulk and the mixture mean form an obtuse angle in the whitened geometry. The whitened cosine measures that angle. Constraining the signs of loadings, covariances or means does not cure it; a positive N for every pair of positive vectors would need a precision matrix that maps the positive orthant into itself, which a covariance estimate has no reason to satisfy.
Why the factor aligned with the mean flips the sign. On raw counts the first factor of a type is close to its mean, so write \boldsymbol{\Sigma}=\boldsymbol{\Delta}+\nu\,\boldsymbol{m}\boldsymbol{m}^{\top} with \boldsymbol{\Delta}\succ0 and \tau=\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{m}. The Sherman–Morrison identity gives

\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}
=\frac{\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}}{1+\nu\tau}.
\tag{5.5}
Exact alignment attenuates N but keeps its sign when \boldsymbol{\Delta} is diagonal and \boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{y}>0. The sign flips under near alignment: if the factor is \rho\boldsymbol{m}+\boldsymbol{u} with \boldsymbol{u} small and nearly orthogonal to \boldsymbol{m}, the high-variance direction removes almost all the weight of the mean, and N is set by \boldsymbol{u}, by the other factors and by the bulk–reference mismatch in those directions. Shrinkage helps for a geometric reason, not by repairing an eigenvalue: as \lambda\to1 the precision tends to a positive diagonal \boldsymbol{W}, and then N=\sum_g w_g m_g y_g>0.
Cell size in the model. If a cell of type j is \boldsymbol{x}_c=s_c\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_c, with s_c the size factor (\mathrm{E}\,s_c=1, \operatorname{Var}s_c=\nu_j), its covariance holds \nu_j\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top}. Transferred whole to the bulk, that term says that the overall magnitude of the bulk is very uncertain, while that magnitude is what identifies c: the parameters stay identifiable, but the data carry little information on c. Two choices are defensible.

If the size variation is mostly technical and specific to the reference platform, transfer only the residual “shape” covariance, \sum_jp_j\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol{x}_c-s_c\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}), and model the bulk sampling noise apart. The size-normalised input of Section 4.1.1 approximates it.
If it is biological and adds up in a physical sum of cells, keep \sum_jp_j\nu_j\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}^{\top} as an explicit variance component, but then c needs information from outside the mean direction that this component down-weights: an external n_i, or a capture ratio shared by several bulks.

A size estimate defined by the mean, \hat s_c=\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{x}_c/\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}\boldsymbol{H}\boldsymbol{\mu} with \boldsymbol{H} a diagonal weight, then a factor model of \boldsymbol{x}_c-\hat s_c\boldsymbol{\mu}, removes that direction more precisely than dropping the first empirical factor. It is not implemented here.
Constrained profile. At fixed \boldsymbol{p} the residual quadratic form is convex in c, so the maximum over c\ge0 is \max(0,\hat c). For c>0 strictly there is no interior maximiser when \hat c\le0: the supremum is at c\downarrow0. A floor c_{\min}>0 therefore marks a boundary, not a fit; and a softplus or log parameterisation of c keeps the iterates legal but sends c to zero when the likelihood prefers a negative value. It does not create information.
Diagnostics. For each fit, record

N_c=\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{y},\qquad
D_c=\boldsymbol{m}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{m},\qquad
\cos_W(\boldsymbol{m},\boldsymbol{y})
=\frac{N_c}{\sqrt{D_c\,\boldsymbol{y}^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}\boldsymbol{y}}},
\tag{5.6}
the information on c, I_c(\boldsymbol{p})\propto D_c, and, for each loading \boldsymbol{b}_{jk}, its alignment with the standardised mean, A_{jk}=\lvert\boldsymbol{b}_{jk}^{\top}\boldsymbol{D}_j^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\rvert/
(\lVert\boldsymbol{b}_{jk}\rVert\,\lVert\boldsymbol{D}_j^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}\rVert). A negative \cos_W shows that the failure is an angle, not a non-positive eigenvalue; A_{jk} near 1 marks a size factor able to remove most of the information on c. 5.3.5 Four scale models
fit_decovart_scales() and scales_given_terms() (R/04_02_stats_sieve_multivariate.R) fit the three replicates of one time × condition together under one of four scale models. For replicate i, with the terms of Equation 5.4 at its composition and Q_i=\boldsymbol{y}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol{W}_i\boldsymbol{y}_i, the log-likelihood without its constant is

\ell_i=-\frac{G}{2}\log\phi_i-\frac12\log\det\boldsymbol{S}_W(\boldsymbol{p}_i)
-\frac{Q_i-2c_iN_i+c_i^{2}D_i}{2\phi_i}.
\tag{5.7}

Free (the DeCovarT profile, used so far): c_i=N_i/D_i, \phi_i the residual over G. c_i can be negative, and the fit then stops.
Positive: c_i=\max(c_{\min},N_i/D_i), with c_{\min} one thousandth of the total-count scale \boldsymbol{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{y}_i/\boldsymbol{1}^{\top}\boldsymbol{m}_i, and \phi_i recomputed at that c_i. A replicate at the bound is flagged.
Linked: c_i=a\,n_i and \phi_i=a^{2}n_i=a\,c_i, with the capture ratio a shared by the three replicates and one cell count n_i per replicate. At fixed a, N_i drops out of the score in c_i, whose root is

c_i=\frac{-Ga+\sqrt{G^{2}a^{2}+4D_iQ_i}}{2D_i}>0
\tag{5.8}
(ledger R5, verification/sympy/check_covariance_selection.py); a maximises the summed likelihood (Brent’s method on \log a).
Shared c: the replicates are first scaled to their median library depth, then share one c, with \phi_i free; coordinate ascent alternates c=\sum_iN_i/\phi_i\big/\sum_iD_i/\phi_i (at least c_{\min}) and \phi_i. After depth scaling, c is common only up to the composition-weighted cell size \sum_jp_{ji}S_j, with S_j the panel total per cell of type j (its transcriptome size on the panel): replicates with different compositions do not have exactly the same c.

The three constrained models alternate a composition step (each replicate by DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell() at fixed scales, L-BFGS-B) and a scale step; the summed likelihood increases at every step. With a free for each sample, (a_i,n_i) is only a reparameterisation of (c_i,\phi_i), since a_i=\phi_i/c_i and n_i=c_i^{2}/\phi_i: only sharing a, or knowing n_i, adds information.






NoteThe cell count of a bulk sample is not known



n_i, the number of cells in each Suppinger bulk sample, is not reported. An external count, the gastruloids per sample (96) times the cells per gastruloid at each time (Suppinger et al. 2023, STAR Methods, p. 25), would let n_i enter the linked model as an offset (\log n_i fixed, only a free) or as a prior on \log n_i centred on that count. 5.3.9 Six directions to improve the estimates
Ranked by the evidence of this benchmark, with the perspectives of the DeCovarT article in mind (its section “Improve DeCovarT”). Each item states what was observed here and what is only expected.

Choose the regularisation of the covariance for the deconvolution, not for the covariance.

Observed: \lambda=0.5 divides the RMSE by ten at 96 h on the Welch panel (Figure 5.2); the denoised covariance, which is the least regularised input, is the worst.
Done: the level is chosen without the observed composition on the real bulks (Section 5.3.3), and the factor form \boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{B}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{\Psi} is screened with constrained scales on pseudo-bulks (Section 5.3.6) and on the real bulks (Section 5.3.8). Still to do: an extended rank grid, one level common to the types against one per type in the bulk likelihood, and the sparse precisions of chapter 3.
Expected, not shown: a common level matters more than its value.








Note 5.1: Regularisation visualisations still to add





A review of chapters 3 and 4 (lasso_regularisation.md, not part of the book) proposes figures that link the covariance geometry, the regularisation level, the bulk likelihood and the deconvolution error. Its priorities, in order: correlation and partial-correlation heatmaps; eigenvalue spectra and conditioning; a map of the per-type (held-out cells) against the common (bulk) level; the bulk likelihood when the level of one type moves at a time, the others fixed at the common level and \boldsymbol{p}, c, \phi refitted; gene-wise bulk residual heatmaps; the stability of the chosen level; likelihood gain against composition error. Shrinkage towards the identity does not impose sparsity, so a partial-correlation map is the conditional association under the fitted Gaussian law, not a regulatory network. Per-type regularisation map: per-type level chosen on held-out cells against the common level chosen by the bulk likelihood (Figure 5.11; one page per time in output/deconvolution/figures/regularisation/regularisation_map_welch.pdf).

Still to do from the review: partial correlations from the full-panel precision, the one-type-at-a-time bulk likelihood, residual heatmaps and the stability of the chosen level (item 6 below).




Estimate the composition from the mean equation: quasi-likelihood, GEE, Fisher scoring.

Observed: the QP with the full raw covariance (0.060) against the likelihood on the same plug-ins (0.36), and the full-likelihood stage undoing the QP (Figure 5.16).
The quasi-score \boldsymbol{D}^{\top}\boldsymbol{V}_0^{-1}\{\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{m}(\boldsymbol{p})\}
=\boldsymbol{0} stays unbiased when the working covariance is wrong; the likelihood does not. Its iteration is the IRLS of the article, and the QP stage here is that iteration with a non-negativity constraint.
Inference then needs a sandwich. With one bulk the genes are the only units and they are correlated: HC3 as a leave-one-gene-out jackknife is too narrow, and a jackknife over clusters of the precision graph is the natural version for DeCovarT.
Stacking the covariance equation on the mean equation (GMM) would bring back the term that failed here; it should come with a weight chosen from the data, not at full weight.

Treat close types as a lineage.

Observed: after summing the paraxial mesoderm, 17 of 18 methods are within 0.04 on the Welch panel (Table 5.9, Figure 5.4); the mean profiles have a cosine similarity of 0.99 (Figure 5.3).
To do: a two-level fit (lineage first, then the split inside it on the genes that separate its members), or a penalty on the split, or archetypes along the differentiation axis instead of discrete types.
This is the direction with the least dependence on the estimator: it helps every method of the table.

Add a measurement layer between the single-cell reference and the bulk.

Observed: correlation 0.48 to 0.83 between a bulk and its own reference mixture; \hat n<1; Huber weights help the diagonal QP (0.105 → 0.039 at 96 h); the DeMixSC residual weights are among the best comparators; dividing the bulk by b_g helps on the small panels and hurts on the Welch panel at 96 h.
Not supported as implemented: one variance scale per gene, pooled over six bulks (stage qp_means_var).
To do: a gene-wise mean–variance law across bulks, \operatorname{Var}(y_{gi})=\omega m_{gi}+\kappa_g m_{gi}^{2}, with \kappa_g a negative binomial dispersion, which is the marginal law of a Poisson log-normal model (Equation 4.4), or a mixed model with a gene random effect shared by the bulks of one platform. A full multivariate Poisson log-normal convolution has no closed form; its first two moments are enough for item 2.

Carry the precision of the reference, with replicates or a jackknife; do not refit the reference from the bulk.

Observed: MEAD weights genes by the variance of the type means across (pseudo-)individuals and is the best comparator at 96 h on the Welch panel (0.048); refining the means from one bulk is the worst stage (0.50).
To do: a delete-a-group jackknife of the cells of each type for the variance of \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j} and of \hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_j, used as weights and in the sandwich of item 2; the two cell lines at 48 h for a first estimate of the between-replicate layer; a mean refinement only when it is shared by many bulks.

Select the level on further bulk profiles.

Observed: three replicates per protocol and time. That is too few for an 80/20 split of the bulks without regenerating pseudo-bulks, and too few independent biological replicates for a stability analysis of the chosen level.
To do, if more bulk profiles become available: the profile log-likelihood of each held-out bulk at every candidate level, fitted on the others; the spread of the maximising level across bulks then measures how stable the choice is.


Not in the list, on this evidence: the Firth penalty and the between-type covariance term (no consistent effect), and other optimisers (the optimiser is not what fails).

5.4 Glossary
The terms underlined in this chapter, with the definitions of glossary/glossary.yml.




Table 5.16: Glossary of the terms used in this chapter.






term
definition




Aitchison distance
The Euclidean distance between two compositions after the centred log-ratio transform. It weighs relative errors, so a small type counts as much as a large one.


aliquot
A physical split of one specimen, so a bulk library and a single-cell library measure the same material.


arm
One way of regularising the covariance of each cell type, with its own tuning value: shrinkage towards the variances, the two-parameter family, or a factor model. The deconvolution model stays the same in every arm.


capture ratio
The factor that takes a reference count onto the scale of the bulk. The mean grows with the product of this factor and the cell count. The within-type covariance grows with its square times the cell count.


cell count
The number n of cells whose transcripts make up one bulk sample. It is not measured for the Suppinger bulks, so it is only known through c and phi.


cell size
The total transcript content of a cell. Its counts are the biological size times the technical capture, so the two cannot be told apart from counts alone.


coefficient of variation
Standard deviation divided by the mean. For a count it falls as the mean grows, so it compares the spread of genes or samples measured on different scales.


deviance share
The fraction of a gene's Poisson deviance explained by the cell types, written R2_D. The panels keep the Welch-gated genes with R2_D of at least 1% or 5%.


factor loading
A column of the matrix B in the covariance B B' + Psi: the weights with which one latent factor moves the genes together.


Frobenius risk
The expected sum, over every gene pair, of the squared error of that covariance entry. A variance and a covariance count the same.


grid search
Scoring every value of a fixed list of tuning values and keeping the best. With one or two tuning parameters it is as reliable as random search.


held-out log-score
The Gaussian log-density of cells left out of the fit, averaged over them. A higher value means the covariance estimated without them predicts them better.


mean scale
The number c that takes the reference mixture mean to the scale of the bulk. Physically, the capture ratio times the number of cells in the bulk, c = a n.


negative binomial dispersion
The factor in the variance mean plus dispersion times mean squared. Here it is biological variability of the expression or of the size factor.


nested cross-validation
Two loops of cross-validation: the inner loop chooses the tuning value on the training cells only, and the outer loop scores that choice on cells the inner loop never saw.


platform ratio
The gene-wise ratio of a bulk count to the reference mixture at the observed composition. It measures how differently the two protocols capture each gene.


profile likelihood
The likelihood maximised over the nuisance parameters, here the two scales c and phi, at each value of the parameters of interest.


proportion
The fraction of cells of one type. It is the weight of that type in the mixture.


pseudo-bulk
A sum of reference cells drawn at a chosen composition. It has the capture of the single-cell platform and a known composition.


restricted likelihood
The likelihood of the residuals once the mean coefficients are integrated out. Its variance estimate divides by the number of genes minus the number of types.


RMSE
Root mean squared error between estimated and observed proportions, over the cell types of a sample.


shrinkage intensity
The number between 0 and 1 that multiplies the sample correlations of a type. At 0 they are kept. At 1 only the variances remain.


size factor
The multiplier of a cell's whole library: the number of transcripts the cell holds (biological) times the fraction of them that the protocol captures and sequences (technical). It moves every gene of the cell together.


uniqueness
The diagonal Psi of a factor model: the variance of each gene that the shared factors do not explain.


variance scale
The number phi that multiplies the mixture covariance of the reference to give the covariance of the bulk. Physically, phi = a squared times n.


Welch panel
The genes that differ between cell types by a permuted Welch test at a false discovery rate of 5%, after the presence gate. The largest of the three gene panels.


whitened cosine
The cosine between the bulk and the mixture mean after both are multiplied by the inverse square root of the bulk covariance. A negative value gives a negative mean scale even when the covariance is positive definite.

text:
6.1 Biological insights from deconvolution algorithms applied to mouse gastruloids
Figure 6.1 contrasts a standard Wnt pulse at 48 h with a premature pulse at 24 h, at three bulk-matched time points: 48 h, 72 h and 96 h. Section 6.1.1 says what the figure can and cannot support; 1 gives the biological reading.

title: 6  Early versus standard Wnt
text:
6.1.1 The figure and its statistical reading






Figure 6.1: Deconvolution-guided comparison of standard versus early Wnt gastruloids at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h.





Figure 6.1 is a raster illustration, not a plot of estimates. Panels A and B draw trajectories; the six bar thumbnails of panel C carry no axis, scale or value. No deconvolution output exists in this repository yet: the comparator runs of Section 5.2 are planned, not run. What follows reads the figure qualitatively and lists what its claims would need. Readings marked (ours) are not in the figure.

The consensus is on direction, not on point estimates. Panel C reports that BayesPrism, SCDC and DWLS agree on the direction of change between arms (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down in the early arm) and not on absolute abundances. Only that direction is carried into



Why absolute abundances disagree. The figure attributes the disagreement to weighted least squares and marker weighting, which are sensitive to collinearity among closely related states. When neighbouring states have close mean profiles on the panel (candidates here, not yet checked: naïve, exiting naïve and epiblast at 48 h; pre-somitic mesoderm and somite differentiation front at 96 h), the signature is ill-conditioned, and a small change of gene weights moves mass between neighbours (3.1, condition number). (Ours.) Collinearity affects every method that inverts the same signature, BayesPrism included; it separates methods only through their weights. Panel C groups SCDC, a weighted least squares, with BayesPrism, a multinomial likelihood, and sets DWLS apart, which points at the dampened weights of DWLS (Tsoucas et al. 2019) rather than at least squares as such. Testing this needs the condition number of the panel signature at each time and the per-method estimates.
Why direction can agree when levels do not. (Ours.) At one time both arms are deconvolved with the same reference and panel. A method bias that multiplies the proportion of a type by a fixed factor cancels in the log-ratio contrast between arms; a bias that moves mass between collinear neighbours depends on the sample and does not cancel. Proportions are also closed: a rise of ectopic pluripotency forces other types down, so “ectopic pluripotency up” and “primitive streak down” are not two independent findings. The redraw therefore reads contrasts on centred log-ratios within each sample.
Uncertainty the claims need. (Ours.)

A per-algorithm interval for every proportion: from the method’s own uncertainty model where it has one (BayesPrism samples a posterior), and from resampling reference cells within type otherwise, which also carries the uncertainty of the one-specimen reference (Section 2.1).
A bootstrap over bulk replicates within arm and time, since the replicate is the unit of the arm effect, not the gene or the cell. There are three replicates per arm and time (Figure 2.1), so a resample takes only 10 distinct values per arm; the redraw shows the nine pairwise early-minus-standard differences beside the percentile interval.
Panel C also states that control gastruloids vary more. A variance from three replicates has two degrees of freedom, and its 95 % chi-square interval spans a factor of about 150, so that claim needs more replicates or a model that pools across types and times.

How to read agreement across methods. (Ours.) The methods share the reference, the panel and the bulk, so their errors are correlated, and agreement of three methods is not three independent confirmations. Two failure modes are shared by all of them. The early-Wnt bulk has no single-cell counterpart at any time (Section 3.4), so a state specific to that arm is forced onto the nearest reference types. And several states drawn in panels A and B (caudal epiblast, neuromesodermal progenitors) are not among the scored reference types of Table 3.2, so no deconvolution against those references can return them. Sign agreement across methods is therefore necessary, not sufficient. A proposed reporting rule for the redraw: call a direction when every method gives the same sign and, for each method, the nine replicate pairs share that sign; report a per-sample goodness of fit on the early arm beside it.



6.1.2 Biological interpretation
On the control-like arm, 72 h is primitive-streak enriched and 96 h shows pre-somitic mesoderm and somite progression. On the early Wnt arm, 48 h retains more naïve pluripotency, 72 h is dominated by ectopic pluripotency with a reduced primitive streak, and 96 h nearly loses pre-somitic mesoderm. Absolute abundances disagree across algorithms (Section 6.1.1), so we treat the direction of change (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down) as the consensus, not the point estimates.

title: 7  Sensitivity analyses
text:
7.2 scDesign3 settings for GSE229513
The fitted count simulator of S5, simulator draws reference-like cells whose type-level law is known. On Suppinger it is used to calibrate, not to resample: the cells of one specimen series are not biological replicates (Note 3.1).



Table 7.1: scDesign3 settings per type and time for GSE229513.









Setting
Value




Fit unit
One model per time slot, 48 h, 72 h and 96 h; the two lines pooled at 48 h, cell line not a covariate (Section 2.1)


Cells and genes
Cells after QC, culture-stress labels removed (Section 3.2); the selected panel, raw UMI counts (Section 4.1.1)


Margins
Negative binomial, mean and dispersion by cell type, log size factor as mean offset; no zero inflation (?nte-drop-zico)


Copula
Gaussian, one per type, correlation of the plug-in \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of that type and time (Section 4.2.1); not refitted


Composition and depth
Type proportions C_j/\sum_\ell C_\ell of the slot, frozen; each synthetic cell takes the size factor of a real cell of its type


Truth for scoring
Count-scale mean and covariance of a large draw (for example 10^{5} cells per type), not \boldsymbol{R}_j


Checks before use
Normal QQ plots of randomised quantile residuals per gene and type; marginal and copula AIC and BIC against independence and the empirical copula






Factors of the list above that the simulator serves:

1, observation noise: negative-binomial cells replace the Gaussian law; pseudo-bulks are sums of simulated cells at known \boldsymbol{p}.
2, missing component: simulate every type and leave one out of the signature.
3, copula dependence: swap the plug-in correlation for an equicorrelated or a Clayton copula, margins fixed.
6, wrong covariance reference: generate with the \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} of one estimator or time, and fit DeCovarT with another.

Spillover (4) and outlier genes (5) are added after generation; the simulator plays no part in them.

text:
7.3 Signature size and selection threshold
S5i, signature size states the hypothesis: accuracy rises with the number of genes, reaches a plateau, then falls once uninformative genes or genes inconsistent between bulk and single-cell libraries enter the panel. Every chapter of this book so far uses one panel, the top n_genes_global = 500 of the legacy type-equal SCTransform ratio (legacy type-equal ratio, Section 3.6). This section plans the sweep that tests the hypothesis on GSE229513. It has not been run.



Table 7.2: Factors of the panel-size sweep. The largest panel stays below the size of the allow-list of every slot (Section 3.2).









Factor
Levels




Panel size n_genes_global
50; 100; 200; 500; 1000; 2000, the top genes of each rank


Rank
legacy type-equal ratio (ranks_global_equal_type.csv, column rank); omnibus rank, cell-weighted deviance R^2_D (column deviance_r2, Section 3.3.2)


Omnibus gate
Benjamini–Hochberg level fdr of rank_genes_omnibus(): 0.001; 0.01; 0.05; 0.2


Bulk consistency filter
off; on (Section 3.4)

Methods
NNLS; DeCovarT, profile Newton (Section 5.2)






Design choices:

Source of genes. The 500-gene export data/intermediate/equal_type_top500_by_time.rds cannot supply panels larger than 500. The sweep reads the allow-list object data/intermediate/suppinger_sct_allowlist_seurat.rds and the full rank table, then subsets genes per panel size.
Truth. Within each type, cells are split at random into a reference half and a pseudo-bulk half. The rank, the mean and the covariance use the reference half only; pseudo-bulks are sums of cells of the other half at known numbers per type. Bulk and reference cells are then disjoint, the condition under which a within-type variance can matter (S5, ReDeconv). Both halves come from one specimen series, so the pseudo-bulks carry no platform bias and no between-specimen variation (Note 3.1).
Platform-inconsistent genes. The pseudo-bulks cannot reveal them. The real standard-Wnt bulks of GSE229386 enter through the bulk consistency filter: the sweep is repeated on the panels with the flagged genes removed, and on the real bulks the change of \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} with panel size is reported, since no truth exists there.
Scale. Means, covariances and pseudo-bulks use raw UMI counts, so a pseudo-bulk is an exact sum of the cell profiles. The size-factor scale of Section 4.1.1 is a second arm.
Metrics. DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics() with the true cell fractions: total variation and RMSE per bulk (regression$global), and per-type correlation and error (regression$cell_type). For the real bulks, the total variation between \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} at each size and at 500 genes.

The covariance has G(G+1)/2 entries per type. Above the number of reference cells of a type the sample covariance is singular, and only a regularised estimate of Section 4.2.1 is defined. The closed-form intensity of this sketch is archived; the sweep should use the level chosen on held-out cells or by the bulk likelihood (Section 5.3.3).
TODO, partly superseded by Section 5.3.3, which sweeps the shrinkage level, the two-parameter arm and factor ranks on the real bulks: add the level of covariance regularisation as a factor of the sweep. The shrinkage estimate is dense by construction: it multiplies every sample correlation by 1 - \lambda and sets none to zero, so it says nothing about isolated groups of genes. At the closed-form intensity the abundant types are barely shrunk (\lambda of 0.006 to 0.03 on the Welch-gated panels, output/grn/plugin/plugin_summary.csv). Levels to compare: (i) \lambda on a grid, closed form; 0.25; 0.5; 0.75; 1 (diagonal, no gene-gene term); (ii) a sparse arm, the graphical lasso precision of Equation 4.1 along its penalty path; (iii) raw counts against size-factor-scaled counts, since a shared cell-size factor correlates every pair of genes. Report, per type and level, the share of non-zero off-diagonal partial correlations, the number of connected components and the condition number, next to the accuracy metrics and the agreement between the two optimisers. Done so far (Section 5.3.2): level (i) for DeCovarT on the raw covariance, L-BFGS-B, bulk as is; the RMSE at 96 h on the Welch-gated panel goes from 0.36 (closed form) to 0.034 (\lambda=0.5), with no gain on the small panels. Levels (ii) and (iii), and a choice of \lambda that does not use the observed composition, remain.

# Not run. Function names and arguments follow R/02_02_stats_cross_cell.R,
# R/03_01_stats_covariance_estimation.R and the DeCovarT reference.
# Culture-stress labels are removed first, as in
# scripts/01_03_export_equal_type_seurat.R.
source("R/02_00_utils.R")
source("R/02_01_stats_quality_control.R")
source("R/02_02_stats_cross_cell.R")
source("R/03_01_stats_covariance_estimation.R")

seu <- readRDS("data/intermediate/suppinger_sct_allowlist_seurat.rds")
ranks <- utils::read.csv(
  "output/naive_marker_selection/tables/ranks_global_equal_type.csv"
)
panel_sizes <- c(50L, 100L, 200L, 500L, 1000L, 2000L)
bh_levels <- c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2)
time_level <- "48h"
n_bulk <- 100L
n_cells_bulk <- 500L

counts <- assay_matrix(seu, "RNA", "counts")
in_slot <- seu$time_point == time_level # & !culture-stress label
x <- as.matrix(counts[, in_slot])
cell_type <- droplevels(factor(seu$celltypeannotation[in_slot]))
lib <- 10^seu$log_umi[in_slot]
types <- levels(cell_type)

# Disjoint halves within each type: 1 = reference, 2 = pseudo-bulk.
half <- withr::with_seed(20261101, {
  stats::ave(
    seq_along(cell_type),
    cell_type,
    FUN = function(i) sample(rep_len(1:2, length(i)))
  )
})
ref <- half == 1L

# Rank A: legacy type-equal ratio of the current panel (computed on all
# cells of the slot; rank B below is the leakage-free one).
rank_a <- ranks[ranks$time_point == time_level & !is.na(ranks$rank), ]
rank_a <- rank_a$gene[order(rank_a$rank)]

# Rank B: omnibus rank on the reference half; fdr = 1 keeps every gene
# so that each BH level is a filter of one fit.
omni <- rank_genes_omnibus(
  x[, ref],
  cell_type[ref],
  size_factors = lib[ref] / stats::median(lib[ref]),
  fdr = 1,
  n_select = max(panel_sizes)
)
omni <- omni[!is.na(omni$rank), ]
rank_b <- lapply(bh_levels, function(level) {
  gated <- omni[omni$adj_pval <= level, ]
  gated$gene[order(gated$rank)]
})
names(rank_b) <- paste0("omnibus_fdr_", bh_levels)

# Pseudo-bulks at known cell numbers, from the pseudo-bulk half.
pseudo <- withr::with_seed(20261102, {
  lapply(seq_len(n_bulk), function(b) {
    w <- stats::rgamma(length(types), shape = 2)
    m <- stats::rmultinom(1L, n_cells_bulk, prob = w / sum(w))[, 1L]
    cells <- unlist(lapply(seq_along(types), function(j) {
      pool <- which(!ref & cell_type == types[j])
      pool[sample.int(length(pool), m[j], replace = TRUE)]
    }))
    list(y = rowSums(x[, cells, drop = FALSE]), p = m / sum(m))
  })
})

fit_panel <- function(genes) {
  mu <- vapply(
    types,
    function(j) rowMeans(x[genes, ref & cell_type == j, drop = FALSE]),
    numeric(length(genes))
  )
  sigma <- vapply(
    types,
    function(j) {
      xj <- t(x[genes, ref & cell_type == j, drop = FALSE])
      fit_cov_shrinkage(xj, lambda = shrinkage_lambda_closed_form(xj))$sigma
    },
    matrix(0, length(genes), length(genes))
  )
  scores <- lapply(pseudo, function(pb) {
    y <- pb$y[genes]
    p_nnls <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_ratios_nnls(y, mu)
    p_dcv <- DeCovarT::deconvolute_single_cell(y, mu, sigma)$p
    rbind(
      cbind(
        method = "nnls",
        DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics(
          y, mu, estimated_p = p_nnls, true_ratios = pb$p
        )$regression$global
      ),
      cbind(
        method = "decovart_newton",
        DeCovarT::compute_benchmark_metrics(
          y, mu, estimated_p = p_dcv, true_ratios = pb$p
        )$regression$global
      )
    )
  })
  do.call(rbind, scores)
}

rank_lists <- c(list(type_equal_ratio = rank_a), rank_b)
sweep <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(rank_lists), function(r) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(panel_sizes, function(n) {
    genes <- utils::head(rank_lists[[r]], n)
    if (length(genes) < n) {
      return(NULL) # the gate passes fewer genes than requested
    }
    cbind(rank = r, n_genes_global = n, fit_panel(genes))
  }))
}))

# Bulk consistency filter on the real standard-Wnt bulks of the slot
# (bulk: genes x 3 replicates, same identifiers). sd and n_cells come
# from the reference half; flagged genes are removed before the sweep
# is repeated.
# flags <- bulk_consistency_filter(bulk, mu = mu_all, sd = sd_all,
#                                  n_cells = table(cell_type[ref]))
# rank_lists_clean <- lapply(rank_lists, intersect, flags$gene[flags$keep])


Three outcomes would bear on the hypothesis. A rise and a plateau in both methods, with no decline up to 2000 genes, says that the panel of 500 is not too large for the pseudo-bulks. A decline that disappears after the bulk consistency filter points to platform-inconsistent genes, which only the real bulks can show. A decline in DeCovarT alone, present already on pseudo-bulks, points to the covariance estimate rather than to the genes.

title: 7  Sensitivity analyses
section: 7.4 A paired bulk and single-cell split
text:
7.4 A paired bulk and single-cell split
The Suppinger score compares a deconvolution with the composition of a single-cell reference from the same time. That reference is not a split of the bulk. An aliquot is a physical split of one specimen, so the bulk library and the single-cell library measure the same material. Four constraints decide whether a published set can carry that comparison.

Real bulk and real single-cell counts come from the same specimen, or from a physical split of one suspension.
Sample identifiers can be traced from the bulk to the single-cell library.
A deconvolution of that pair has been published.
Where the only available truth would be the single-cell recovery itself, an independent count (FACS, imaging or histology) is required.

Three sets meet the first three constraints. Citekeys for these papers are not in the bibliography, so each is named with its DOI.
Dong and colleagues (10.1093/bib/bbz166) split a mouse mammary suspension (GEO GSE136148). SCDC, which is already a comparator in this benchmark, was published on that split. Two animals, and the reported truth is the single-cell recovery.
Guo and colleagues (10.1101/gr.278822.123) profiled healthy retina from 24 specimens, taking bulk and single-cell nuclei from the same suspension. DeMixSC, already a comparator here, was published on that series. The bulk accessions are GSE175937.
Dai and colleagues (10.1126/sciadv.adh2588) deconvolved the forebrain organoids of Jourdon and colleagues (10.1038/s41593-023-01399-0). About 60 samples are reported at TD0, TD30 and TD60. A preparation may pool organoids, so a sample is not always one organoid. Access is NIMH Data Archive study 1482.
He and colleagues (10.1038/s41586-020-2536-x) and the BEDwARS analysis of Ghaffari and colleagues (10.1186/s13059-023-03007-7) are not split aliquots: the bulk and the single-cell profiles are not a physical division of one specimen.
